Why two phones expose different sensor lists

Hardware choices and cost tiers: Manufacturers select sensors per model. Budget phones often omit ambient temperature, humidity, pressure, or heart-rate sensors to save BOM cost. Flagships include them. 

Vendor drivers and OEM firmware: The Android sensor HAL (Hardware Abstraction Layer) is implemented by the SoC vendor and OEM. Two phones with the same physical sensor can expose different capabilities (range, resolution, batching) due to driver differences. 

Android version and HAL: Newer Android versions add sensor types (e.g., hinge angle, head tracker). A phone on Android 10 cannot expose sensors added in API 29+ even if hardware exists. 

Region/model variants: The same marketing name can have different sensor suites in different regions (e.g., dual-SIM vs single-SIM variants, regulatory differences). 

Virtual sensors derived from other sensors: Gravity, linear acceleration, rotation vector, and game rotation vector are often fused in software from accelerometer + gyroscope + magnetometer. If a phone lacks a gyroscope, these virtual sensors may be absent or lower quality. 

Emulator vs phone: The Android Emulator provides a fixed, simulated sensor set defined by the AVD image. It does not reflect the diversity of real devices.
Does a reported sensor guarantee useful or accurate measurements?

No. The sensor list and metadata describe capability, not calibration or quality. 

Metadata ≠ calibration: Maximum range, resolution, and power are design specs. A sensor can meet specs yet be poorly calibrated (offset, scale error, cross-axis sensitivity). 

Noise and drift: MEMS sensors exhibit thermal noise, bias drift, and vibration sensitivity. Gyroscopes drift over time; magnetometers distort near metal. 

Placement: A phone in a pocket, hand, or mount sees different dynamics than one on a table. Proximity sensors behave differently when the screen is covered vs. exposed. 

Vendor quality: Two sensors with identical datasheet values can perform differently due to silicon lot, assembly, and driver tuning. 

Accuracy status: Android reports accuracy (UNRELIABLE, LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH) at runtime. A listed sensor may stay at UNRELIABLE if calibration failed. 

Permission and battery limits: Background sensor access is restricted (Android 9+). Throttling can reduce effective rate, making high-rate sensors impractical for continuous use.
When would a sensor add little value to the user task?

The task does not depend on it: If the feature works with user input (e.g., typing a temperature), a sensor adds complexity without benefit. 

User can enter data more reliably: For sparse, subjective, or precise data (e.g., "produce variety", "exact weight"), manual entry beats a noisy sensor. 

Coarse values suffice: If the decision threshold is wide (e.g., "is it day or night?"), a high-resolution light sensor is overkill; a simple time check works. 

Battery cost outweighs benefit: Continuous high-rate sampling (gyroscope at 200 Hz) for a feature used once a day is hard to justify. 

Not widely available: If only 30% of target devices have the sensor, the feature excludes most users unless a robust fallback exists. 

Privacy or policy: Some sensors (heart rate, microphone) require sensitive permissions and user consent, adding friction.

The sensor list is defined by the AVD image and virtual sensors. Values are simulated (often constants or simple patterns). Power, vendor, and resolution fields are generic placeholders. Conclusions about "phones in general" cannot be drawn from the emulator alone. This analysis covers only the inventory observed in this environment.
Battery, availability, and quality checklist before adding a sensor feature

☐ Is the sensor available on ≥80% of target devices? (Check Play Console device catalog) ☐ Does the feature work with on-change or low-rate sampling? (Avoid continuous high-rate) ☐ Can we batch with FIFO / maxDelay to reduce wake-ups? ☐ Is there a graceful fallback (user input, coarse alternative, disable feature)? ☐ Have we tested on real devices across price tiers, not just the emulator? ☐ Does the sensor stay at HIGH accuracy in typical use (case, pocket, mount)? ☐ Is the permission model acceptable (foreground only, no body sensors unless essential)? ☐ Can the user calibrate or override (e.g., "lighting is fine, take photo anyway")?
